title: About
text:
This project is part of Guillermo Garcia Costoya’s research on natural selection in Anolis lizards, advised by James Stroud. Fieldwork took place on Lizard Island.
The source code for this site, the cleaned data and the analysis scripts are in the GitHub repository.

title: 4. Fit
text:
Planned contents

Fitting M1 and M2 to the analysis dataset (computed in scripts/, results saved to results/).
Sampler diagnostics: divergences, \(\hat R\), effective sample sizes and energy.
Parameter summaries for performance, survival and detection.
Posterior predictive checks: resighting histories by species and sex, performance distributions, and leaf censoring rates.
Model comparison of M1 and M2 by leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO).

title: 2. Model
text:
Show code
library(tidyverse)
lizards <- read_csv("data/lizards-spring-2024.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
n_missing_morph <- sum(lizards$exclusion == "missing morphology", na.rm = TRUE)
The model estimates both links of the paradigm jointly, morphology → performance and performance → survival, while correcting survival for imperfect detection. The choices behind the data inputs are explained on the Data page. A PDF version of this page is also available.

title: 2. Model
text:
Causal diagram



Causal structure of the model. Solid arrows are present in both models. The dashed arrow (direct effects \(\gamma\)) is present only in M2. Sex affects performance (\(\delta\)), survival (\(c\)) and detection (\(\zeta\)). Body temperature at the trial affects sprint and bite (\(t\)).

title: 2. Model
text:
Transformations
All continuous variables except body temperature are log-transformed. All, including temperature, are then standardised within species, using that species’ observed sample mean and SD: \[
\operatorname{std}_s(v) = \frac{v - \bar{v}_s}{\operatorname{sd}_s(v)}.
\] Coefficients are then in within-species SD units, and so comparable among species and traits. Survival coefficients become standardised selection gradients (on the logit scale), and one set of generic priors can be used. The constants \(\bar v_s\) and \(\operatorname{sd}_s(v)\) are fixed data, so the simulator used for calibration applies the identical transformation (prepare_data() in R/prepare-data.R).

title: 2. Model
text:
Performance submodel
Each lizard’s vector of the four performance traits is multivariate normal: \[
\mathbf{u}_i \sim \operatorname{MVN}\left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{s[i]}\right),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_s = \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_s)\, \boldsymbol{\Omega}\, \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_s),
\] with a mean that depends on size, the linked shape trait, sex and body temperature: \[
\mu_{ij} = \alpha_{sj} + \delta_{sj}\, m_i + b^{\text{svl}}_{sj}\, x_{i,\text{svl}} + b^{\text{shape}}_{sj}\, x_{i,k(j)} + t_{sj}\, w_{ij}.
\]

\(\alpha_{sj}\) is the expected performance of a female of average size and shape, tested at the species’ mean temperature.
\(t_{sj}\) is the effect of body temperature during the trial. It is estimated for sprint and bite only, and fixed at 0 for both clinging traits. Temperature is a condition of the trial, not a trait of the lizard. Survival therefore depends on temperature-adjusted performance, \(\tilde u_{ij} = u_{ij} - t_{sj}\, w_{ij}\): the lizard’s expected performance at its species’ mean test temperature.
\(\delta_{sj}\) is the male–female difference in performance not explained by morphology.
\(b^{\text{svl}}_{sj}\) and \(b^{\text{shape}}_{sj}\) are the size and shape effects on performance (the first link of the paradigm).
\(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\) is a residual correlation matrix shared across species. It captures lizards that perform well on all tasks for reasons beyond the measured morphology, such as condition or motivation.
Missing \(u_{ij}\) are parameters drawn from the same distribution, so lizards with missing performance still contribute their survival information. This assumes values are missing at random given morphology, sex and the other performance traits.
Leaf-clinging zeros are left-censored. For those lizards, \(u_{i,\text{leaf}}\) is also a parameter, but it is constrained to lie below the detection limit, \[
u_{i,\text{leaf}} < c_s = \operatorname{std}_s(\log 0.01),
\] and follows the same multivariate normal distribution. They therefore count as the weakest leaf clingers, rather than being dropped or given an arbitrary value. The standardisation constants for leaf clinging are computed from the non-zero values.

title: 2. Model
text:
Survival and detection submodel
The probability of surviving the first six months depends on temperature-adjusted performance: \[
z_i \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(\phi_i),
\] \[
\operatorname{logit}(\phi_i) = a_s + c_s\, m_i + \sum_j \beta_{sj}\, \tilde u_{ij} + \sum_j q_{sj}\, \tilde u_{ij}^2 \;\left[\, + \sum_k \gamma_{sk}\, x_{ik} \,\right]_{\text{M2 only}}.
\]

\(a_s\) is the logit 6-month survival of an average female.
\(c_s\) is the sex difference in survival.
\(\beta_{sj}\) is linear selection on performance \(j\), and \(q_{sj}\) is quadratic selection. \(q < 0\) is stabilising and \(q > 0\) disruptive. The conventional quadratic gradient is \(2q_{sj}\).
\(\gamma_{sk}\) is the direct effect of morphology on survival. It is fixed at 0 in M1. Including \(x_{i,\text{svl}}\) here guards against attributing size-related survival to performance.
Correlational selection (\(\tilde u_{ij} \tilde u_{ij'}\) terms) is not included.

Resighting depends on whether the lizard is alive: \[
y_{i2} \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(z_i\, p_i), \qquad \operatorname{logit}(p_i) = \pi_s + \zeta_p\, m_i,
\] \[
y_{i3} \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(z_i\, \lambda_i), \qquad \operatorname{logit}(\lambda_i) = \ell_s + \zeta_\lambda\, m_i.
\]

\(p_i\) is the probability of detection in fall given the lizard is alive.
\(\lambda_i\) is the probability of being seen in spring 2025 given the lizard was alive in fall. It combines fall-to-spring survival and spring detection, which three occasions cannot separate. It is a nuisance parameter.
The sex effects on detection, \(\zeta_p\) and \(\zeta_\lambda\), are shared across species. Males display and may be more conspicuous.

This is a Cormack–Jolly–Seber model for three occasions. Summing over the latent \(z_i\) gives the likelihood of each history:



History \((y_{i2}, y_{i3})\)
Probability




1 1
\(\phi_i\, p_i\, \lambda_i\)


0 1
\(\phi_i\, (1 - p_i)\, \lambda_i\)


1 0
\(\phi_i\, p_i\, (1 - \lambda_i)\)


0 0
\((1 - \phi_i) + \phi_i\, (1 - p_i)(1 - \lambda_i)\)



Lizards seen in spring 2025 but missed in fall (history 01) identify \(p\). Selection on 6-month survival (\(\phi\)) is then estimated free of detection bias. This assumes detection does not depend on performance or morphology beyond sex.

title: 2. Model
text:
Derived quantities
For morphological predictor \(k\) in species \(s\), evaluated at the species mean, where \(\tilde u = 0\) so the quadratic terms vanish: \[
\text{indirect}_{sk} = \sum_{j} b_{sjk}\, \beta_{sj},
\qquad
\text{direct}_{sk} = \gamma_{sk},
\qquad
\text{total}_{sk} = \text{indirect}_{sk} + \text{direct}_{sk}.
\] Here \(b_{sjk}\) is \(b^{\text{svl}}_{sj}\) for \(k = \text{svl}\), \(b^{\text{shape}}_{sj}\) when \(k = k(j)\), and 0 otherwise. Size is the only predictor with indirect paths through all four performance traits. Support for full mediation is assessed in three ways: from the posteriors of \(\gamma_{sk}\), by comparing M1 and M2 with PSIS-LOO, and by checking in simulation (Validation) whether the design can detect \(\gamma \neq 0\).

title: 2. Model
text:
Priors

Hierarchical structure
Every parameter labelled hierarchical below varies by species and is partially pooled: \[
\theta_s = \mu_\theta + \tau_\theta\, \tilde\theta_s, \qquad \tilde\theta_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1),
\] with separate \(\mu_\theta\) and \(\tau_\theta\) for each performance trait \(j\) or predictor \(k\). This is the non-centered form used in Stan. With only three species, \(\tau_\theta\) is weakly identified, so its priors are deliberately informative.


Prior distributions
All scales are standardised traits or logits. \(\mathcal{N}^+\) is the half-normal distribution.

The reasoning behind these priors:

Performance intercepts \(\alpha_{sj}\) are near 0 by construction, because traits are centred within species. They are offset only by the sex term, so pooling them adds nothing. A first version used \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1)\), but prior predictive simulation showed it allowed implausible shifts in performance, for example leaf censoring rates above 30% when about 3% is observed. It was tightened to \(\mathcal{N}(0, 0.5)\).
Performance slopes of \(\mathcal{N}(0, 0.5)\) put 95% of the mass below about 1 SD of performance per SD of morphology.
Residual SDs \(\sigma_{sj}\) must lie below 1, because performance is standardised.
Baseline survival \(\mu_a \sim \mathcal{N}(-1, 1)\) centres 6-month survival near 27%. That is a little above the naive 20%, as expected once detection is accounted for.
Selection gradients of \(\mathcal{N}(0, 0.5)\) allow odds of survival to change up to about 2.7-fold per SD of performance (2 prior SDs). The quadratic terms are tighter.
Detection intercepts of \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1.5)\) are close to uniform on the probability scale.

Prior predictive checks of these priors are on the Validation page.

title: 2. Model
text:
Assumptions and limitations

Performance and morphology are measured without error. Sprint timing resolution violates this mildly.
Missing data. Performance is missing at random given the model. The 17 lizards with missing toepad area or hind toe length are excluded. Only one of them survived to 6 months.
Detection depends on species and sex only. Movement off the study area is indistinguishable from death, so \(\phi\) is apparent survival.
Shared residual correlation. The correlation among performance traits, \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}\), is the same for all species.
Temperature. Its effect on performance is linear, and it is unmeasured for both clinging trials.
Claw size. Relative hind toe length is a stand-in for claw size.
No correlational selection. It could be added as an extension.
Three species. Among-species variances are estimated mostly from their priors.

title: Start here
text: This site is the complete, open record of a study of natural selection in three Anolis lizards on Lizard Island. Every step is here, from the cleaned field data to the final biological conclusions: data cleaning decisions, model equations, Stan code, validation and model checks. The pages are meant to be read in order, but each one stands on its own.

title: Start here
text:
The question
Many evolutionary studies link morphology directly to survival or reproductive success. The ecomorphological paradigm proposes a middle step instead: morphology determines what an animal can do, its whole-organism performance, and performance determines whether it survives.





flowchart LR
  M[Morphology] --> P[Performance] --> S[Survival] --> R[Resighting]
  M -.-> S


 The paradigm being tested. Solid arrows are the mediated path; the dashed arrow is a direct effect of morphology on survival that bypasses measured performance. 



We test two hypotheses:

M1, full mediation. Morphology affects 6-month survival only through sprint speed, bite force and clinging ability on bark and on leaves.
M2, partial mediation. Morphology also affects survival directly, through routes that measured performance does not capture.

title: Start here
text:
Study system
Lizards were captured, measured, tested for performance and individually marked in spring 2024, then resighted in fall 2024 (6 months) and spring 2025 (12 months). We analyse three species that share the island:



Species
Abbreviation




Anolis carolinensis
caro


Anolis cristatellus
cris


Anolis sagrei
sag



Survival is never observed directly, only resightings. Lizards that are alive can be missed, and how often differs among species. The model therefore estimates detection probability alongside survival.

title: Start here
text:
Reproducing the analysis
The repository contains everything needed to reproduce the results from the cleaned data:
data/        cleaned analysis dataset and capture summary
R/           shared functions: data preparation, priors, simulator, plot theme
stan/        Stan model (in progress)
scripts/     long computations (SBC, model fits), saved to results/
figures/     static figures (causal diagram)
*.qmd        the pages of this site
To rebuild the site, clone the repository, install the R packages loaded in R/ and the pages, and run quarto render. Heavy computations (simulation-based calibration and model fits) are run separately from scripts/, and their saved outputs are read by the pages.

title: Start here
text:
Data availability
The analysis uses data/lizards-spring-2024.csv, which has one row per lizard marked in spring 2024. It includes every correction and exclusion as columns (corrections, exclusion), so each cleaning decision on the Data page can be traced. The raw field data are not part of the public repository. The cleaned file is produced from them by R/process-raw-data.R, which is included so that every cleaning step is documented.

title: 1. Data
text:
Show code
library(tidyverse)
source("R/prepare-data.R")
source("R/plot-theme.R")

lizards <- read_csv("data/lizards-spring-2024.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, levels = species_levels))
captures <- read_csv("data/capture-summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
analysis <- lizards |> filter(is.na(exclusion))
This page goes from the field data to the dataset the model uses. Every correction and exclusion is listed with its reason, and the plots show the patterns that motivated the modelling choices on the Model page.

title: 1. Data
text:
Field data
Lizards were captured in three censuses. Only in spring 2024 were lizards measured, performance-tested and marked. The fall 2024 census (6 months later) recorded only captures. Spring 2025 (12 months) is available only as a resighted/not-resighted record for each marked lizard.


Show code
captures |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = season,
    values_from = c(captures, recaptures_of_spring_lizards)
  ) |>
  transmute(
    species,
    `spring 2024 captures` = `captures_spring 2024`,
    `fall 2024 captures` = `captures_fall 2024`,
    `of which recaptures` = `recaptures_of_spring_lizards_fall 2024`
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

The analysis uses the three focal species. Two other species were also marked but cannot support the analysis:

A. distichus (16 lizards) had only 2 survivors.
A. equestris (11 lizards) has no sprint or bite data. It is also far larger (SVL 116–149 mm) than the focal species (about 40–65 mm).

title: 1. Data
text:
Morphology
Raw linear measurements mostly measure body size. Within each species, every raw trait correlates strongly with snout–vent length (SVL). We therefore separate size, measured as log SVL, from shape, measured as size-corrected traits. Shape is the log trait minus log SVL, or minus 2 × log SVL for areas.


Show code
morph_long <- lizards |>
  filter(!exclusion %in% c("no tag", "tag shared by two lizards")) |>
  transmute(
    species, svl,
    `hindlimb (mm)` = hindlimb,
    `head width (mm)` = head_width,
    `hind toe (mm)` = hind_toe_recorded,
    `toepad area (mm²)` = toepad_area,
    flagged = is.na(hind_toe) & !is.na(hind_toe_recorded)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(species, svl, flagged), names_to = "trait") |>
  mutate(flagged = flagged & trait == "hind toe (mm)") |>
  filter(!is.na(value))

ggplot(morph_long, aes(svl, value, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(data = \(d) filter(d, !flagged), size = 1.2, alpha = 0.5, stroke = 0) +
  geom_point(data = \(d) filter(d, flagged), shape = 4, size = 2.5, stroke = 0.9, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~trait, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_species() +
  labs(x = "SVL (mm)", y = NULL) +
  theme_lizard() +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 2.5, alpha = 1)))








Figure 1: Morphological traits against SVL (log scales). Traits scale tightly with size, so raw traits mostly re-measure body size. Crosses mark the hind toe lengths set to missing as implausibly short.

\(\log(\text{fore} + \text{hind toepad area}) - 2 \log \text{SVL}\)
clinging on leaves



The reasons for these choices:

Composite limb lengths. forelimb and hindlimb are exact sums of their upper and lower segments, so segments and totals cannot be included together.
Head length is dropped. In A. carolinensis (\(n = 47\)), relative head length correlates strongly with relative head width and with SVL. With so few lizards, both head traits could not be separated.
Claws. Clinging to rough bark relies mainly on claws, and clinging to smooth leaves on adhesive toepads. Claws were not measured, so relative hind toe length stands in for claw size.
Toepads. Fore and hind toepad areas are summed into a single total.
Implausibly short hind toes. Twelve hind toe lengths were implausibly short, for example 1.0–3.9 mm in lizards of about 43 mm SVL whose toes are typically about 7 mm. They are set to missing when the robust within-species \(z\)-score (median and MAD) of log hind toe − log SVL is below −5. The values show a clear gap: flagged lizards lie between −7.4 and −37, and the next lowest is −4.0.
No PCA. With one or two predictors per performance trait there is no dimensionality problem to solve. Principal components would also mix size and shape back together, and their loadings, and so their meaning, would differ among species.

  filter(!is.na(sprint)) |>

Some features of these distributions shape the model:

Leaf-clinging zeros. 22 lizards scored 0 on leaves. The smallest non-zero value is 0.01, the resolution of the instrument, so a zero means “below 0.01” rather than no clinging at all. The model treats these values as left-censored, estimating each somewhere below the limit.
Why not log(x + 1). The common alternative of adding a constant before taking logs does not work here. For values this small, log(x + 1) is nearly the raw value (correlation 0.996), and the skew barely changes: 4.4 raw and 3.5 after the transform, compared with 0.8 for log of the non-zero values. Results would also depend on the arbitrary constant.
Sprint speed has a heavy lower tail. 8 lizards are more than 3 SD below their species × sex mean, down to 9.7 cm/s. These are probably trials where the lizard did not run properly. The model currently uses normal residuals; heavier-tailed (Student-t) residuals are a possible extension.
Sprint speed is coarsely measured. There are only 29 distinct sprint values, consistent with a fixed track length timed in coarse steps. Near 150 cm/s this is about ±10% rounding.

Survival and resighting
Each lizard has a resighting history: whether it was seen in fall 2024 (\(y_2\)) and whether it was seen in spring 2025 (\(y_3\)). The recorded “6-month survival” is 1 if the lizard was seen at either census. It therefore counts a lizard that was alive but never seen again as dead.


Show code

  mutate(history = paste0(seen_fall, surv_12m)) |>
  count(species, history) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = history, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(
    `naive 6-month survival` = sprintf("%.2f", (`01` + `10` + `11`) / (`00` + `01` + `10` + `11`)),
    `fall miss rate` = sprintf("%d/%d = %.2f", `01`, `01` + `11`, `01` / (`01` + `11`))
  ) |>

title: 3. Validation
text:
NoteIn progress



This page will be filled in once the Stan model is written. The simulator it relies on is already in R/simulate.R.

title: 3. Validation
text:
Planned contents

The simulator. It conditions on the observed design: species, sex, standardised morphology, trial body temperatures and the observed pattern of missing performance. From that design it draws parameters from the priors (R/priors.R), then performance, survival and resightings. Recovery checks confirm that it generates data consistent with the model’s likelihood.
Prior predictive checks. Simulated resighting rates, naive survival, leaf censoring and performance distributions are compared with the observed data, to confirm the priors are plausible but not restrictive.
Simulation-based calibration (SBC) for M1 and M2, shown as rank histograms and ECDF difference plots for every parameter, together with sampler diagnostics.
Power to detect direct effects. How often the posterior for \(\gamma\) excludes 0 when the true direct effect is biologically meaningful, given the sample sizes.

title: 5. Synthesis
text:
Planned contents

Direct vs. indirect effects of each morphological trait on survival, per species: is morphology’s effect mediated by performance?
Morphology → performance: size and shape effects on sprint, bite and clinging.
Selection on performance: survival as a function of each performance trait (linear and quadratic selection).
Species comparison and the role of detection: detection-corrected vs. naive survival.
Interpretation, limitations and next steps, including claw measurements and heavier-tailed sprint residuals.
